chapter: Reading bands and the jazz scene
title: Piron's polished band for the better class
summary: Piron's arrangements demanded note-for-note playing for society audiences, unlike the rougher dance-hall bands, with Handy's halls named.

story.theme_name: Dance halls, lake camps and riverboat bandstands
story.community_name: Dance halls, lake resorts and where bands played

blocks.x: Well, you could get in there like that. But, uh, I knew he'd play them. He was Edward Quest as far.
And other of his music he was, wrote there to play strictly about his music. And he was playing out there at Transcenius and, uh, and, uh, he was playing for the better class of...

and they didn't go for too much of that, you know, rock music, so all this stuff was smooth and soft, things like that. Then he had you playing it note for note and crescendos and different things. That's the way you wanted it played, and that's the way you had to play it for him. So for you to go sit in his band, you understand what I mean. You got to be a pretty polished musician to go sit in his band.
Well, who liked jazz music in those days, say in the 20s when you were here?
Well, practically everybody around here. You wanted to like that because...
Did you say P-Ron would play for a special class of people though, huh?

Yeah, he played for the better class of people, see. He played for the doctors and the lawyers and people up here on St. Charles Street, people back in the place and all that kind of people, the higher class of people, see. And they liked that sweet music and slow and waltzes a lot of things, you know, something like that. Well, the average band around here didn't play that, see. Like John Robeshoe and P-Ron. And they had another fellow here called Peter Bocard and his bunch. Now they played all that kind of music. But we went on down and got on the gutter. Bounced them around a little bit. Well, that's what they liked. We used to go down to the old Corporate's Hall down there and start playing down there around 8 o'clock. And he'd do it at the night and play until 2 or 4 o'clock the next morning. Corporate's, the economy. And then, uh, uh, uh, Sanderson, yeah, he was there then. And they had another hall up there on Howard Avenue. It's just back in the yard. I forgets the name of that. I know we come down here from Baton Rouge to play a contest against, uh, Celestan over there. And I believe that was the first time a lot of those guys heard me play clarinet was in Celestan's band at that time. Who won the contest? Tup. Tup. Tup Johnson won it.
